div.span: Both traditions emphasize God’s love, mercy, justice, and grace, yet diverge in the mechanism by which these attributes operaten
- and s
ince our purpose in life is directly related to God's soteriology, these differences reveal several significant observations at the fundamental level.

Most notably, Christianity distinguishes between law and grace, while Islam does not. In Christianity, the law condemns while grace saves; in Islam, God and His law fully governs both salvation and condemnation - opening the door to forgiveness before punishment by His grace. In Christianity, Adam was punished for his sin; in Islam, he was forgiven. And in Christianity, salvific forgiveness requires God to fulfill the burden

on our behalf, while in Islam, we are held fully accountable to both our sins and righteousness (without any part of the burden being transferred to another) - with God's mechanism for forgiveness established through Adam from the start.

div.font: From the lens of effectiveness, these differences reveal that Islam’s salvific narrative accomplishes everything Christianity’s does, but more consistently. It preserves justice by holding deeds accountable, while manifesting mercy without original sin, vicarious substitution, God becoming a man, or a law that is framed primarily against us - avoiding the portrayal of God in a pagan way, His justice with deflected accountability, and His law negatively - all just to heighten God’s love that was already there (in Islam's narrative). Put differently: if original sin and atonement are removed from the Christian narrative (since atonement is a response to sin’s asymmetrical gravity), the Islamic narrative becomes exposed.

Finally, this comparison also allows us to identify which religion looks more like a corruption of the other - with Christianity diminishing the salvific function of our good deeds and introducing an intermediary between us and God in the form of a man - which is indistinguishable from Satan's goal of getting us to worship creation instead of the Creator. Moreover, Islam's God better fits the concept of a "loving father": He reminded Adam about Satan, taught him of the consequences for both sin and righteousness, and forgave him upon his sincere repentance - just as a loving father would to a righteous and sincerely repentant child for his first offense.

div.span: If the True religion must be distinguishable from falsehood, it will maximize internal and external consistency; and as with each prior section, Islam appears superior to Christianity in this respect.

switch.text: As with prior sections, all results converge on the same observation: Islam delivers a more internally and externally consistent message while achieving the same intended outcome Christianity seeks: justice alongside mercy....
